before: switch selects a case based on an integral or enum value. case 1 labels the instructions for the value 1.
break exits this switch. Without it, execution can continue into following case instructions, even if their labels do not equal the original value.
default handles an input with no matching case label. It is separate from the numbered choices.
This beginner example uses break on each case to avoid accidental fallthrough. Do not remove a break unless continuing into the next block is the intended behavior.
Expected output or behavior: Write. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Trace a valid choice and an unknown choice. Explain why the break after a case matters before experimenting with intentional fallthrough. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: switch compares a value with its case labels. In this example, each label is a whole number. case 1 marks where to start when the choice is one.
break leaves the switch. This stops the program from carrying on through the instructions in the next case.
default marks where to start if no case matches. Here it provides a help message for an unknown choice.
Fallthrough means continuing from one case into the next case's instructions. It can happen without break, even though the next label does not match. This example uses break to prevent it.
The program prints Write. choice is two, so execution starts at case 2. Its break leaves the switch before the Help message.
A case label chooses a starting point. It does not create an automatic stopping point. Read the instructions from that label until a break, return, or the end of the switch.
